comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: One can perhaps describe the ethnic mix on Mauritius a bit like the Dutch describe distribution of religious confessions in Holland. They all wear orange and cheer on the national football team. They live in peace and tolerance. But most villages and small towns are either 100% Dutch Reformed or 100% Roman Catholic. The Dutch say they live "naast elkaar, niet samen" - next to each other, but not together. Bravo to Mauritius for making a silk purse from a sow's ear. The next step: perhaps some kind of organsation or use of cutting edge technology that nobody has thought of yet?

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That Dutch comparison is a sharp one - genuine peace and shared national pride existing alongside quiet, persistent separateness at the community level. "Naast elkaar, niet samen" captures something a lot of multicultural societies wrestle with. Thank you for the thoughtful framing.

comments.author: @deirdrelewis1454
comments.text: Calling Mauritius an African country isn’t really accurate. Yes, Africans were brought in and settled eventually. But that is true of every other group living there today. When the first people arrived, there was no indigenous population. They don’t regard themselves as African.

Geography is based on continental shelf and region, no who got there first, lacking a precolonial indeginous population doesnt erase geography or statehood, infact Mauritius is member of African Union and an African Country, end of story!

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: Fair point to raise - Mauritius's population is entirely descended from post-17th-century settlement and migration (African, Indian, Chinese, and European), with no pre-existing indigenous group, which does make its national identity fit awkwardly into standard regional categories. Worth being precise about that distinction.
